title: Effects of Longitudinal Spin Current Density Gradient on Spin-Orbit Torque Switching of Perpendicular Magnetization
authors: Guowen Gong, Qianbiao Liu, Lijun Zhu
abstract: It has remained a critical open question as to whether a longitudinal spin current gradient (e.g., due to a gradient in the thickness, composition, or width) can replace the longitudinal magnetic field required for deterministic spin-orbit torque switching of normal metal/ferromagnet heterostructures with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Here, we report robust micromagnetic and experimental evidence that any realistic longitudinal spin-current density gradient cannot be an effective replacement for a longitudinal magnetic field to enable deterministic switching of a perpendicular magnetic anisotropy device. Instead, the longitudinal spin current density can only modify the nucleation and pulse-timing-sensitive oscillations of magnetic domains and thus the picosecond-scale strip-like indeterministic switching windows. The same conclusions hold robustly when the transverse effective field associated with the spin-current pulse (the sum of the Oersted field and field-like torque) is taken into account. The indeterministic switching prevents applications in the presence of finite device-to-device variations and drifts in write current pulse and thermal fluctuations of device parameters. We also experimentally show that, instead of a longitudinal spin current density gradient, perpendicular spins are much more effective in deterministic switching of perpendicular spin torque devices.
summary: This work addresses the critical question of whether a longitudinal spin current gradient can substitute for an external longitudinal magnetic field to deterministically switch perpendicular magnetization in magnetic heterostructures. Through micromagnetic simulations and experiments, the authors demonstrate that gradients are insufficient, concluding that deterministic switching requires a longitudinal field or, alternatively, perpendicular spin components.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether a longitudinal spin current density gradient can replace the longitudinal magnetic field required for achieving deterministic spin-orbit torque (SOT) switching in perpendicular magnetic anisotropy (PMA) heterostructures.
main_result: The study concludes that any realistic longitudinal spin current density gradient is insufficient to enable deterministic switching, as the switching remains highly indeterministic and sensitive to device variations. Perpendicular spins are shown to be a much more effective mechanism for deterministic switching.
method: The research combines micromagnetic simulations with experimental measurements on NM/FM bilayers to analyze magnetization dynamics under varying current and field conditions.
model_or_system: The system under study is a normal metal/ferromagnet (NM/FM) bilayer exhibiting PMA. The dynamics are governed by spin-orbit torques derived from spin currents, considering both uniform and gradient components.
key_observables: Out-of-plane component of magnetization ($m_z$), switching probability, and the time-revolved evolution of $m_z$ during SOT switching.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that deterministic switching requires an effective longitudinal magnetic field, and the authors note that observed switching in literature might stem from mechanisms other than simple longitudinal spin current gradients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematics of gradient generation, the time-resolved evolution of $m_z$ under uniform vs. gradient currents, and phase diagrams showing the dependence of the final switching state on current density and gradient strength.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the open question regarding gradient replacement for $H_x$, presents micromagnetic simulations showing the failure of gradients to induce deterministic switching, and concludes with experimental evidence contrasting gradient effects with the superior performance of perpendicular spin generation.
why_interesting: While focused on spintronics, the analysis of non-equilibrium dynamics, phase transitions (switching), and the role of engineered gradients in controlling magnetization reversal shares conceptual overlap with understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems.
